Linear homogeneous DE of order n with constant coefficients
We consider linear homogeneous differential equation of order n with constant coefficients

                   L(y) ≡y (n)(x) + a1y (n−1)(x) + ... + an−1y ′(x) + any(x) = 0,                  (1)

where a1, ..., an are real constants. At the last lecture we defined the characteristic polynomial

                            p(λ) = λn + a1λn−1 + ... + an−1λ + an                             (2)

and the characteristic equation

                             λn + a1λn−1 + ... + an−1λ + an = 0.                              (3)

We proved that the function exp(λx) is a solution of DE (1) if λ is a root of the characteristic
polynomial p(λ) in (2) or the same the characteristic equation (3).





Alexander Gladkov, Professor  (Belarusian State University)                 DIFFERENTIAL EQUATIONS                                  September 16, 2026                 3 / 48

Now we will suppose that characteristic polynomial (or the same the characteristic equation) has
complex roots.
The complex conjugate root theorem states that if p is a polynomial in one variable with real
coefficients, and a + ib is a root of p with a and b real numbers (b ̸= 0 ), then its complex conjugate
a −ib is also a root of p.
Moreover, if a + ib is the root of multiplicity k, then its complex conjugate a −ib is also the root of the
same multiplicity k.
Thus the roots of the characteristic polynomial p whose imaginary parts do not vanish occur in
conjugate pairs.  If λi is a complex root of multiplicity mi then its complex conjugate λi is a root with
the same multiplicity mi. Let us enumerate the roots of the characteristic polynomial p as follows:

                                λ1, λ1, λ2, λ2, .... λj, λj, λ2j+1, ..., λs,

where
                       λk = αk + iβk,   (k = 1, ..., j, αk, βk ∈R, βk ̸= 0)

and λ2j+1, ..., λs are real. Suppose that λk has multiplicity mk. From the Fundamental Theorem of
Algebra we have





Alexander Gladkov, Professor  (Belarusian State University)                 DIFFERENTIAL EQUATIONS                                  September 16, 2026                 5 / 48

To find the roots of the characteristic equation we need some information about roots of complex
numbers.

We can write any complex number in algebraic form z = x + yi. An alternative option for coordinates in
the complex plane is the polar coordinate system that uses the distance of the point z from the origin
O, and the angle subtended between the positive real axis and the line segment Oz in a
counterclockwise sense. This leads to the polar form of complex numbers. The absolute value (or
modulus) of a complex number z = x + yi is

                                                   r = |z| = p x2 + y 2.

If z is a real number (that is, if y = 0), then r = |x|. That is, the absolute value of a real number equals
its absolute value as a complex number.





Alexander Gladkov, Professor  (Belarusian State University)                 DIFFERENTIAL EQUATIONS                                  September 16, 2026                13 / 48

The argument of z (in many applications
   referred to as the ”phase” ϕ) is the angle of
   the positive real axis with the radius Oz, and is
   written as ϕ = arg(z). Together, r and ϕ give
   another way of representing complex numbers

               z = r(cos ϕ + i sin ϕ).

   This is trigonometric form  of complex
  numbers.

The Cauchy-Euler equation
In the preceding section we have seen how to obtain the general solution of the n-th order linear
homogeneous differential equation with constant coefficients. The general n-th order linear equation
with variable coefficients is quite a different matter, however, and only in certain special cases can the
general solution be obtained explicitly in closed form. One such special case of considerable practical
importance is the so-called Cauchy-Euler equation. It is sometimes referred to as an equidimensional
equation. This is an equation of the form

                a0xny (n)(x) + a1xn−1y (n−1)(x) + ... + an−1xy ′(x) + any(x) = f (x),             (10)

where a0, a1, ..., an are real constants, f (x) is a continuous function.
THEOREM 4.
The transformation x = exp t reduces the Cauchy-Euler equation (10) to a linear differential equation
with constant coefficients.
Proof. We will prove this theorem for the case of the second-order Cauchy-Euler differential equation

                             a0x2y ′′(x) + a1xy ′(x) + a2y(x) = f (x).                          (11)

                                  dt2    dt        dt

or
                                 d2y     dy

                                      dt2      dt





Alexander Gladkov, Professor  (Belarusian State University)                 DIFFERENTIAL EQUATIONS                                  September 16, 2026                21 / 48

where b1 = a1 −a0, g(t) = f (exp t). This is a second-order linear differential equation with constant
coefficients, which was what we wished to show. Theorem is proved.

REMARK.
1. Note that the leading coefficient a0xn in DE (10) is zero for x = 0. Thus the basic interval I referred
to in the Existence and uniqueness theorem, does not include x = 0.
2. Observe that in the above proof we assumed that x > 0. If x < 0, the substitution x = −exp t is
actually the correct one. Unless the contrary is explicitly stated, we will assume x > 0 when finding the
general solution of a Cauchy-Euler differential equation.

To find rational roots for of the characteristic equations we proved a simple test in the last lecture.
THEOREM.
If a polynomial with integer coefficients

                      P(x) = a0xn + a1xn−1 + a2xn−2 + ... + an−1x + an

has a rational root x0 = p/q (p/q is not cancellable fraction) then the number q is a divisor of the
number a0, and the number p is a divisor of the number an.





Alexander Gladkov, Professor  (Belarusian State University)                 DIFFERENTIAL EQUATIONS                                  September 16, 2026                35 / 48

following rational roots
                                   ±1, ±2, ±3, ±6.

By inspection we find that λ1 = 1 is a root of the equation (21). Dividing polynomial in the left-hand
side of (21) by λ −1, we obtain

                   λ4 −7λ3 + 17λ2 −17λ + 6 = (λ −1)(λ3 −6λ2 + 11λ −6).

To find rational roots of the following cubic equation

                                   λ3 −6λ2 + 11λ −6 = 0                                  (22)
